docs.intro.page: game-kit is a kit for assembling desk games: the physical mechanics of a desk, not a UI
library and not a game. A deck, a hand, a zone, a card you can pick up and put down.
Rules — whose turn it is, what beats what, who has won — are layered on top later, as
configuration. None of them are in here.
## Three planes
Everything in the kit belongs to exactly one of three, and most of the design follows from
keeping them apart.
- **Spec** — what an author writes. It is data: it travels the wire and it is saved. A card is
1×1 units and wears a `plate` surface because somebody said so.
- **State** — what happens. The card moved, the hand was dealt, the zone was emptied.
- **Viewer** — who is looking. Dark or light, the HUD etalon, the debug outlines. Two players
can hold different values over one truth, so nothing here reaches state, and no node is ever
asked about it.
## Nodes and atoms
There is one entity — a node: an `id` and a place among other nodes. A bare node is valid, not
a stub. Everything else is an atom, a small interface composed in at construction.
```ts
node("card", Bounded(), Surfaced())     // a box, and something to paint on it
node("desk", Container(), Surfaced())  // no box of its own; the area comes from content
node("marker")                          // valid, and invisible
Nothing extends anything: there is no base class and no kind field. Behaviour asks for the
atom it needs — hit-testing for a box, painting for a surface — never for a category. Compose
an atom whose requirement is missing and it is not disabled but absent; the tree tells you
what it lacked.
## Units, not pixels
Sizes in the model are in units. The host is the only part that knows what a unit is worth on
the current screen, so one spec looks right on every device.
## How to read this catalog
The sidebar is a ladder rather than an alphabet, and each rung is one atom:
1. **Node** — an id and a place. Nothing is drawn.
2. **Bounded** — a box. Room is taken; still nothing is drawn.
3. **Surfaced** — a surface. Now there is something to see.
4. **Transformable** — a pose: where a node sits, how high it stands.
5. **Container** — the first rung with more than one node: how children are arranged.
Two tools sit beside every scene. The **node tree** — a panel next to Controls in story mode,
a block under the canvas on a docs page — shows what the model actually holds; on the first
rungs, where nothing is drawn, it is the only thing to read. The scene's own toolbar carries
settings of that one canvas: the HUD etalon, and **bounds**, which outlines every box.
**Controls** are the atom's fields. Change a size, a layout or a name and both the picture and
the tree follow — which is what makes this a catalog rather than a page of screenshots.
